This is a draft companion map based on the author's supplied master scope and subsequent sequencing decisions. It is not a replacement textbook scope, an adopted assessment outline or a set of verified device operating instructions. Vendor/runtime setup, local conditions and event hours require local confirmation.

Keep the two calendars separate

  • General textbook: 64 teaching slots per unit across Weeks 1–16, with examinations separately in Weeks 17–18.
  • Local Unit 1 draft: 64 entries include four Week 9 event-reference checkpoints and three Week 16 examination blocks. The remaining 57 entries include teaching, preparation and controlled tasks; they are not all new-content lessons.
  • Week 9: four checkpoints organise references across a proposed two-day event. They are not four additional 55-minute periods or proof that two event days fit into four ordinary periods. Record actual contact hours and the lessons replaced.
  • Week 16: L1 is preparation; L2–L4 model one 150-minute paper plus 15 minutes administration across three 55-minute blocks. Confirm a suitable continuous session, reading-time requirements and school arrangements; separated ordinary periods are not assumed sufficient.

The applied drone/VR engine plus 2D hackathon is a proposed local two-part architecture. Reconcile its common criteria, contributions, individual evidence and total time before issue. Do not automatically add the general textbook's standalone project on top.

LOCAL COMPANION · UNIT 1

Drone programming, 2D hackathon and physical networking

Mapping status: Draft 64-entry Unit 1 lesson crosswalk available; equipment procedures and event/contact-hour budget still need local confirmation.

General readings: Your first Python program · Making decisions with selection · Repeating work with loops · Functions and scope · Working with one-dimensional arrays · Text files and reliable input · Designing and testing solutions · Network foundations · Addresses, devices and media · Designing and protecting a network

Teaching flow: General programming explanation -> predicted trace -> taught adapter/replayed telemetry -> expected/actual comparison -> changed textbook task. Later networking uses the same address/device/diagnostic concepts.

Assessment boundary: The proposed local applied-engine component and hackathon component belong to a reconciled local task architecture. The textbook standalone Pygame project is a separate example; do not add its workload or marks automatically.

Accessible alternative: Python text-only engine, synthetic telemetry and ordinary 2D project; supplied network evidence for conceptual work.

Before issuing the local task: Confirm adapter/runtime contract, observed versus simulated evidence, individual explanation/change task, component contributions and the event/exam calendar.

LOCAL COMPANION · UNIT 2

Pod/security scenarios and a relational database

Mapping status: SQL-strand weekly planning is available; a complete local security/cipher/privacy lesson crosswalk remains to be checked.

General readings: Relational database foundations · Modelling entities and relationships · Normalisation · Getting started with SQL · Building a database solution · Threats and protective measures · Responsible data use

Teaching flow: General database/security reading -> supplied records or logs -> guided practice -> changed independent attempt -> feedback before the local practical.

Assessment boundary: If the practical is in Week 10, its SQL operations must be taught and practised earlier. Do not copy a plan that leaves first SELECT teaching until after the practical.

Accessible alternative: SQLite fixtures on ordinary computers; synthetic security cases and offline policy tests.

Before issuing the local task: Confirm assessed operations, normalisation/CREATE prerequisites, constraint tests, recovery evidence and any server-driver differences. Keep non-SQL content inside the same lesson budget.

LOCAL COMPANION · UNIT 3

VR/spatial OOP, advanced 2D hackathon and network performance

Mapping status: Concept/equipment bridge available; a full local 64-entry lesson crosswalk and timing trial are not yet completed.

General readings: Rebuilding Python fluency · Advanced data structures · Searching: linear and binary · Sorting algorithms · Objects and classes in Python · Extending object-oriented design · Developing a software solution · Network models and protocols · Addressing and subnetting · Designing secure networks

Teaching flow: General objects/grids/dictionaries/algorithm explanation -> small ordinary Python example -> taught spatial/2D implementation -> individual state/algorithm explanation -> changed core task.

Assessment boundary: Retain the proposed applied VR engine plus hackathon relationship as a local option. Vendor APIs, coordinate dimensions, rendering and first-use integration require their own preparation if retained in the task.

Accessible alternative: Ordinary Python classes and a 2D scene or console model; synthetic timings/network traces.

Before issuing the local task: Confirm the actual supported runtime/API, platform language bridge, accessible alternative, independent authentication and total project/event time. A headset outcome does not replace algorithm evidence.

LOCAL COMPANION · UNIT 4

Database/application integration and security on pods/servers

Mapping status: SQL-strand weekly planning is available; full local integration/security lesson mapping and workload trial remain pending.

General readings: Refining relational database designs · Advanced SQL queries · Database development and evaluation · Cyber security analysis · Security controls and responses · Secure communication and cryptography · Ethical and legal considerations

Teaching flow: General multi-table/schema/ACID/security concept -> SQLite practice -> explicitly taught driver/server adaptation -> requirement-linked test, recovery and justified evaluation.

Assessment boundary: Core ACID concepts remain syllabus-linked. Explicit driver/transaction syntax and supporting LEFT JOIN/HAVING material need teaching before they are required by a local task.

Accessible alternative: SQLite plus an ordinary Python application, fictional booking data, local role/policy models and paper analysis.

Before issuing the local task: Verify driver placeholders, data types, transaction boundaries, constraints/cascade behaviour, import decisions and actual recovery tests; do not infer equivalence from successful connection alone.

Mapping still to complete

Unit 1 has a draft lesson-level crosswalk. Units 2 and 4 have provisional SQL-strand weekly allocations, not complete security/integration crosswalks. Unit 3 currently has a concept/equipment bridge, not a completed 64-entry local lesson map. The general planner and topic support cover all four units while this companion grows.

Use the current SQL pathway: Year 11 SELECT/filter/order -> known-key joins -> all five aggregates -> design/CREATE -> INSERT/integrity -> controlled UPDATE/DELETE -> independent rehearsal/feedback. Year 12 then extends the core reports/schema/import work. Teach any retained supporting extension before assessing it.

Unit 2 · provisional SQL-strand weekly allocation

This is a strand plan within four ordinary lesson slots, not four extra SQL lessons. Complete the non-SQL crosswalk before calling it a full local unit plan. Group filters, outer joins and driver-specific syntax shown in local examples do not enlarge the prescribed SQL keyword list; keep the current SQL pathway's core/extension distinction.

Local week 1 · Database vocabulary, records/fields/types; inspect a supplied relational fixture

Relational database foundations → Start with a question · Relational database foundations → Turn records into information · Relational database foundations → Database, DBMS and RDBMS

Practice: Distinguish a raw record from a useful report. Use a supplied fixture before expecting students to create a schema.

Slot budget: 2 database foundation; 1 cybersecurity; 1 guided/independent application

Local week 2 · PK/FK relationships and first SELECT projection

Modelling entities and relationships → From entity to table · Modelling entities and relationships → Choose identifiers deliberately · Modelling entities and relationships → Read relationships in both directions · Getting started with SQL → Choose result columns with SELECT

Practice: Select named fields from one table. Read the relationship before using it later; distinguish projection from deletion.

Slot budget: 2 database/SQL; 1 authentication; 1 practice/check

Local week 3 · WHERE comparisons, literal types and ORDER BY

Getting started with SQL → Filter rows with WHERE · Getting started with SQL → Make order and duplicates deliberate

Practice: Predict and execute a filter/order on fresh rows; show target and excluded rows.

Slot budget: 2 SQL; 1 social-engineering context; 1 independent practice

Local week 4 · AND/OR/NOT, parentheses and LIKE; simple INNER JOIN through known keys

Getting started with SQL → Combine conditions and test boundaries · Building a database solution → Join keys to obtain readable reports

Practice: Compare grouped conditions; manually match parent/child keys before a simple joined report. No multi-table Year 12 complexity.

Slot budget: 2 SQL; 1 threat/malware context; 1 joined-query practice

Local week 5 · Consolidate the taught query operations without adding an unseen test demand

Getting started with SQL → Interpret empty results and debug · Getting started with SQL → Complete the independent query brief · Building a database solution → Join keys to obtain readable reports

Practice: A changed filter/join task uses known tables; feedback names the first wrong condition/key.

Slot budget: 1 cybersecurity theory test; 1 feedback; 1 SQL retrieval; 1 scheduled security/control work

Local week 6 · COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX over the correct records

Building a database solution → Summarise the right records · Building a database solution → Practice and explain

Practice: Predict aggregate outputs from a small fixture before running them. Complex GROUP BY/HAVING remains Year 12 scope; any optional grouping example is labelled.

Slot budget: 2 SQL/aggregates; 1 responsibility/security; 1 independent practice

Local week 7 · Dependencies, anomalies and UNF→1NF→2NF; draft design before CREATE

Normalisation → State the rules before choosing a key · Normalisation → Start with a repeating group · Normalisation → Dependencies explain the next split · Normalisation → 2NF: remove partial dependencies

Practice: Explain the dependency removed at each stage and retain a meaningful relationship. Prepare a proposed project design without pretending this is independently authored final work.

Slot budget: 2 modelling; 1 SQL retrieval; 1 formative project preparation

Local week 8 · 3NF and schema creation; constraints; INSERT parent/child records

Normalisation → 3NF: remove the transitive dependency · Building a database solution → Create and inspect four related tables · Building a database solution → Insert a new record deliberately · Building a database solution → Create a fresh relational database independently

Practice: Independently create a fresh small database, enable actual FK enforcement and test duplicate/orphan/required-value failures.

Slot budget: 1 normalisation; 2 schema/insert practice; 1 independent schema/check

Local week 9 · UPDATE/DELETE with exact WHERE targets; integrate queries and schema skills

Building a database solution → Update the intended row and check it · Building a database solution → Delete only the disposable test record · Building a database solution → Test against requirements, then transfer

Practice: Run a changed mock practical and corrective feedback before Week 10. Scope includes only what has already been explicitly taught and practised.

Slot budget: 2 formal project workshops; 1 safe changes; 1 mock/check and feedback

Local week 10 · SQL practical, then diagnosis; no first teaching of assessed syntax here

Getting started with SQL → Complete the independent query brief · Building a database solution → Test against requirements, then transfer

Practice: 50-minute practical +5 minutes administration. Target list: SELECT, WHERE/Boolean/LIKE, ORDER BY, simple INNER JOIN, aggregates, taught CREATE/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/constraints. Drop any item without prior independent practice evidence.

Slot budget: 1 controlled practical; 1 post-collection feedback; 2 project workshops

Local week 11 · Parameterised application calls for the chosen driver; apply taught database work

Building a database solution → Bridge Python to a controlled SQL change · Building a database solution → Insert a new record deliberately · Building a database solution → Update the intended row and check it

Practice: Separate SQL syntax from bound data; the chosen driver determines placeholders. This is after the practical and is not retroactively added to its scope.

Slot budget: 1 secure application lesson; 3 project workshops

Local week 12 · Project testing and safe backup/restore verification

Building a database solution → Test against requirements, then transfer · Building a database solution → Rehearse and recover with a transaction · Responsible data use → Evaluate the database with evidence

Practice: Open a restored separate copy and query known records. Additional transaction depth/server administration is an extension unless explicitly taught for the local project.

Slot budget: 1 recovery lesson; 3 project workshops

Local week 13 · Finish project demonstration, evidence and evaluation

Building a database solution → Launch, document and evaluate the project · Responsible data use → Evaluate the database with evidence

Practice: Judge against issued criteria using actual query/change/recovery evidence. No new compulsory framework/driver/syntax at the deadline.

Slot budget: 4 project slots including demonstration, evaluation and feedback

Local week 14 · Mixed retrieval and recovery reasoning; optional server extensions separated

Unit 2 integrated review → Integrate and explain · Unit 2 consolidation → Work through targeted stations

Practice: Use changed records/design/security facts to check retained skills. Optional server log replay is not a prerequisite for the default project.

Slot budget: 2 database retrieval/recovery; 2 remaining security/cipher/responsibility consolidation

Local week 15 · Unfamiliar SQL/ERD/normalisation/security exam practice

Unit 2 exam preparation → Use the original practice paper · Unit 2 exam preparation → Bring the specified stimulus · Unit 2 exam preparation → Check, correct and explain limits

Practice: Practice with supplied stimulus, preserve original responses, explain corrections and retry changed cases.

Slot budget: 4 revision/practice/feedback slots

Local week 16 · Formal examination; no essential new SQL teaching

Unit 2 exam preparation → Use the original practice paper · Unit 2 exam preparation → Check, correct and explain limits

Practice: Textbook is preparation/review only during a closed-book examination. Arrange a continuous school-approved session and separate later feedback.

Slot budget: Exam/preparation/administration according to the actual school timetable

Unit 4 · provisional SQL-strand weekly allocation

This is a strand plan within four ordinary lesson slots, not four extra SQL lessons. Complete the non-SQL crosswalk before calling it a full local unit plan. Group filters, outer joins and driver-specific syntax shown in local examples do not enlarge the prescribed SQL keyword list; keep the current SQL pathway's core/extension distinction.

Local week 1 · Diagnose Year 11 keys/SELECT/filter/order/basic joins; repair before extension

Modelling entities and relationships → Choose identifiers deliberately · Getting started with SQL → Choose result columns with SELECT · Getting started with SQL → Filter rows with WHERE · Building a database solution → Join keys to obtain readable reports

Practice: Fresh diagnostic names prerequisite gaps. Use prepared fixtures so server/DDL setup does not block query learning.

Slot budget: 2 SQL retrieval/repair; 1 cryptography; 1 independent practice

Local week 2 · INNER JOIN chains up to four tables, aliases and qualified names

Advanced SQL queries → Define the report’s grain · Advanced SQL queries → Join up to four tables and keep keys visible

Practice: Predict one row per declared report entity and inspect every ON key. Repair missing join conditions without hiding the problem with DISTINCT.

Slot budget: 2 SQL; 1 certificates/trust; 1 independent changed join

Local week 3 · Aggregate at the correct grain; GROUP BY; optional HAVING extension

Advanced SQL queries → Aggregate at the correct grain · Advanced SQL queries → Filter rows and groups deliberately

Practice: Calculate small expected groups manually; distinguish selected attributes, row filters and group filters.

Slot budget: 2 SQL; 1 web-security concepts; 1 grouped report practice

Local week 4 · WHERE versus optional HAVING group filtering; calculated/concatenated fields; NULL semantics

Advanced SQL queries → Calculate and concatenate with aliases · Advanced SQL queries → Respect composite keys and unknown attendance · Advanced SQL queries → Filter rows and groups deliberately

Practice: Use nonzero capacities for percentages, defined NULL meaning and composite-key matches; explain deterministic ordering.

Slot budget: 2 SQL; 1 secure coding; 1 independent changed report

Local week 5 · LEFT JOIN and zero-count reports; filter placement

Advanced SQL queries → Preserve zero-booking sessions · Advanced SQL queries → Respect composite keys and unknown attendance

Practice: Predict an unbooked parent row and compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(non-null child key). Do not conflate a missing record with recorded absence.

Slot budget: 1 security theory test; 1 feedback; 1 SQL model; 1 independent SQL check

Local week 6 · Review CREATE/ALTER/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/constraints, then transactions

Database development and evaluation → Make controlled changes and verify effects · Database development and evaluation → Use transactions to protect a booking · Advanced SQL queries → DDL and DML: change the structure, change the records

Practice: Positive and failed second-step cases demonstrate actual commit/rollback and unchanged non-target rows. Constraints and authorisation are separate.

Slot budget: 2 SQL/transaction lessons; 1 ethics/privacy; 1 independent transaction check

Local week 7 · 3NF, wider ER interpretation and project-sized dictionary/schema reconciliation

Refining relational database designs → Refine from requirements, not a table count · Refining relational database designs → Read the six-table crow’s-foot model · Refining relational database designs → Make a data dictionary that matches implementation · Refining relational database designs → Interpreting a ten-table ER model

Practice: Trace PK/FK/optionality and dependencies; design at the required scale. BCNF/additional server topics are extensions, not hidden replacements for core modelling.

Slot budget: 2 modelling; 1 schema/retrieval; 1 independent design/check

Local week 8 · Python/DBMS connectivity, bound parameters and transaction tests

Database development and evaluation → Use transactions to protect a booking · Database development and evaluation → Verify a parameterised update at the interface · Database development and evaluation → Trace application connectivity through ODBC

Practice: Use the selected driver, trace application/request/result and run a changed mock practical with feedback. sqlite3 is not an ODBC driver.

Slot budget: 1 connectivity; 1 parameterised operations; 1 mock; 1 correction/independent retry

Local week 9 · Launch the database project; integrate already-taught report and change operations

Database development and evaluation → Investigate and design measurable requirements · Advanced SQL queries → Complete the query clinic · Database development and evaluation → Test workflows, failures and reports

Practice: Consolidate a changed dataset before the practical. Read all required operations against the teaching record; no surprise extension item.

Slot budget: 3 project workshops; 1 practical-readiness/retry

Local week 10 · Controlled SQL practical then specific post-collection repair

Advanced SQL queries → Complete the query clinic · Database development and evaluation → Test workflows, failures and reports

Practice: 50-minute practical +5 minutes administration. Candidate scope is taught joins/grouping/HAVING/calculations/NULL/LEFT JOIN/schema changes/transactions; include bound application calls only where independently practised and feasible under the adopted conditions.

Slot budget: 1 practical; 1 post-collection feedback; 2 project workshops

Local week 11 · Project data quality, import and application integration

Database development and evaluation → Clean an import without inventing data · Database development and evaluation → Data quality: five factors in practice · Database development and evaluation → Test workflows, failures and reports

Practice: Preserve raw source, record cleaning decisions and demonstrate an agreed all-or-none failure policy. New import teaching is not claimed as prior Week 10 knowledge.

Slot budget: 1 import/data-quality lesson; 3 project workshops

Local week 12 · Restore/reopen, regression testing and recovery limitations

Database development and evaluation → Preserve a known-good version and prove recovery · Database development and evaluation → Test workflows, failures and reports

Practice: Verify an actual persisted copy and query known contents; distinguish in-memory rollback from durable recovery. Server replay/replication are separate optional cases.

Slot budget: 1 recovery lesson; 3 project workshops

Local week 13 · Finish demonstration/evaluation/handover with no new required dependency

Database development and evaluation → Run the prototype and evaluate its limits · Database development and evaluation → Preserve a known-good version and prove recovery

Practice: Explain independently one report, one rejected operation and one recovery result using the issued scope. Record incomplete criteria honestly.

Slot budget: 4 project slots including demonstration, evaluation and feedback

Local week 14 · Mixed short-answer database/security/programming/network retrieval

Unit 4 integrated review → Predict reports before running SQL · Unit 4 integrated review → Explain transactions, connectivity and recovery · Full-course exam preparation → Read the command and use the stimulus

Practice: Use source facts, command verbs and manual SQL predictions; corrected work remains separate from original timed responses.

Slot budget: 4 exam-practice/retrieval slots

Local week 15 · Extended scenario transfer and delayed retries

Full-course exam preparation → Attempt original mixed practice · Full-course exam preparation → Transfer to a changed case · Full-course consolidation → Show improvement with a fresh and delayed attempt

Practice: Integrate ERDs/3NF/report reasoning and algorithm/security explanations. Dedicated search/sort/Big O teaching must remain in Unit 3, not first appear as revision here.

Slot budget: 4 extended-practice/correction/retry slots

Local week 16 · Formal examination; no essential new SQL teaching

Full-course exam preparation → Prepare against the current instructions · Full-course exam preparation → Make a manageable readiness plan

Practice: Preparation/review references only; no mid-paper book use unless allowed. Confirm a continuous school exam session separately.

Slot budget: Exam/preparation/administration according to the actual school timetable

Unit 1: textbook visit, application and return

The first eight lessons have a printable foundations pack; later programming, network and systems practice is in the activity packs. These support the general concepts but do not certify a particular adapter, drone or pod procedure.

64 local entries

Unit 1 · W1 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Explain inputs, processing, outputs and development requirements

Your first Python program → A problem before a program · Your first Python program → Sequence: follow the order · Designing and testing solutions → Investigate: understand the problem

Textbook visit: Read the badge IPO example; label its requirement before considering any equipment.

Local application: Use three requirement cards: a badge calculator, a drone command sequence and a network service. Identify the shared investigate/design/develop/evaluate process.

Learning check and expected reasoning

For 5 badges at $3 each, name input, processing and output; write one testable requirement.

Expected: 5 is input; multiply by 3; output $15. Requirement describes an observable result for valid quantities.

Unit 1 · W1 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Run a saved program and choose types deliberately

Your first Python program → Prepare your workspace · Values, types and operators → Match the type to the meaning · Values, types and operators → Convert deliberately · Values, types and operators → Calculate and predict

Textbook visit: Run the sequential badge example; inspect types and arithmetic without opening later advanced harnesses.

Local application: Set up the approved editor; modify a simple input/calculation/output program. Inspect a supplied telemetry-style record without connecting hardware.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Predict int('4') * 3 versus '4' * 3, then choose a type for identifier '0042'.

Expected: 12 versus '444'; retain identifier as text to preserve zeros. Save and run the intended file.

Unit 1 · W1 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Translate user needs into testable IPO requirements

Designing and testing solutions → Investigate: understand the problem · Designing and testing solutions → Plan the work and dependencies · Designing and testing solutions → Build and revise a Gantt schedule

Textbook visit: Read requirements and the small Gantt example; distinguish the example schedule from the local assessment calendar.

Local application: Use the planning board to turn an interactive-program brief into inputs, processing, outputs and an eight-slot dependency plan.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Coding takes four rather than three slots after investigation/design. Does the original eight-slot sequential plan still fit?

Expected: No: code 3–6, test 7–8, evaluate 9. Negotiate a justified scope/deadline change rather than silently deleting testing.

Unit 1 · W1 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Trace state, classify a syntax fault and retrieve character representation

Your first Python program → Trace and test · Values, types and operators → Assignment updates a value · Numbers and characters in a computer → Text needs an agreed representation · Numbers and characters in a computer → Apply a character code in three bases

Textbook visit: Trace the sequential example on paper, inspect the expected-result table and complete the B/66 character transfer prompt.

Local application: Dry-run a changed calculation; inspect a deliberately unmatched quote as a syntax example; reserve a short explicit character-code exercise omitted from the master.

Learning check and expected reasoning

For B=66, give eight-bit binary and hex; explain why changing notation does not change the value.

Expected: 01000010 and 42; both represent 66. Code point and UTF-8 byte representation are different concepts.

Unit 1 · W2 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Evaluate comparisons and Boolean conditions

Making decisions with selection → 1. From an instruction to a decision · Making decisions with selection → Combine conditions and choices

Textbook visit: Read how a condition selects a path; inspect the combined-condition example and trace both Boolean inputs.

Local application: Classify sample battery/permission values against an illustrative rule on paper; the rule is not a physical-flight safety specification.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Evaluate battery >= 30 and authorised when battery=29 and authorised=True.

Expected: False: both operands must be true. A successful permission check alone does not establish the threshold.

Unit 1 · W2 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Implement single, dual and nested decisions

Making decisions with selection → 2. Design before coding · Making decisions with selection → 3. Implement the decision in Python · Making decisions with selection → 4. Trace it yourself

Textbook visit: Read design-before-code, the implementation and trace sections; predict before running.

Local application: Write a menu that rejects invalid commands, then distinguishes start/stop/status. Practise one nested condition with an explicit expected path.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Trace -1, 0 and 2 through negative-invalid / zero-empty / otherwise-process branches.

Expected: Exactly one intended branch per input; distinguish an if/elif/else chain from unrelated if statements.

Unit 1 · W2 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Validate a multi-choice command without losing input meaning

Making decisions with selection → Combine conditions and choices · Text files and reliable input → Accept only usable input · Values, types and operators → Convert deliberately

Textbook visit: Read usable-input rules as a targeted prerequisite; use selection to decide on already-converted values before full exception handling is taught.

Local application: Build a text-only command menu with documented accepted spellings. Use supplied conversion scaffolding; hardware calls remain stubbed.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Explain why successful int('-4') conversion is not sufficient range validation.

Expected: It is an integer but may violate the allowed domain. Conversion, range checks and command permission are distinct.

Unit 1 · W2 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Test exact decision boundaries and explain truth tables

Making decisions with selection → 4. Trace it yourself · Making decisions with selection → 5. Test the boundary · Unit 1 consolidation → Station A: Boolean expressions and types

Textbook visit: Inspect boundary-testing guidance and the Boolean station; keep advanced optional code closed.

Local application: Desk-check the command menu with values just inside/outside the agreed range; compare expected paths with actual paths.

Learning check and expected reasoning

For an inclusive permitted range 1–5, give four discriminating tests and expected outcomes.

Expected: 0 reject, 1 accept, 5 accept, 6 reject; typical value 3 alone does not expose endpoint errors.

Unit 1 · W3 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Choose fixed and condition-controlled iteration; launch the applied-engine component

Repeating work with loops → A fixed number of repetitions · Repeating work with loops → Repeat while a condition remains true · Designing and testing solutions → Investigate: understand the problem · Designing and testing solutions → Test: choose evidence that can expose mistakes

Textbook visit: Read loop purposes and test planning; connect one general loop contract to the issued local brief.

Local application: Introduce the drone-engine project requirements and staged evidence. Use a stubbed command sequence first; distinguish formal issue from guided preparation.

Learning check and expected reasoning

When is a while loop preferable to a fixed-count loop, and what must eventually change?

Expected: A condition determines continuation; an update or event must allow termination. Both need stated assumptions and boundary tests.

Unit 1 · W3 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Read an API contract before calling an external component

Designing and testing solutions → Read and use a library API contract · Repeating work with loops → Repeat while a condition remains true · Values, types and operators → Match the type to the meaning

Textbook visit: Read the caller/contract/implementation distinction; identify arguments, response type and failure behaviour in teacher-supplied interface notes.

Local application: Inspect an approved drone connection/SDK demonstration and a provided adapter; learners are not expected to author sockets, classes or functions not yet taught.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Identify what an API contract must state before an illustrative send_command call can be tested.

Expected: Accepted commands/arguments, units, result/error behaviour and version. Do not infer success solely from sending a request.

Unit 1 · W3 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Trace a timed sequence and its stopping condition

Repeating work with loops → Trace the running total · Repeating work with loops → Repeat while a condition remains true · Repeating work with loops → From algorithm to implementation

Textbook visit: Use the running-total trace and pre-test loop explanation; predict each iteration before observing it.

Local application: Run the approved staged drone or simulator sequence through teacher-provided controls; record planned/observed events without importing later modular-design demands.

Learning check and expected reasoning

count=1; while count<=3 outputs count then increments it. List outputs and final count.

Expected: Outputs 1,2,3; final count 4; the last false condition check is not another body execution.

Unit 1 · W3 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Diagnose a loop boundary using expected and actual state

Repeating work with loops → Trace the running total · Repeating work with loops → Test zero, one and several iterations · Designing and testing solutions → Debug: isolate the first incorrect state

Textbook visit: Compare zero/one/several-iteration reasoning with the standard trace; isolate the first mismatch.

Local application: Use a synthetic countdown/battery log; distinguish observed values from a hypothesis about equipment behaviour.

Learning check and expected reasoning

A condition-controlled loop starts with its condition false. How many times does its body run?

Expected: Zero for a pre-test loop; justify from the first check, not from the intended number of commands.

Unit 1 · W4 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Use one-dimensional indexing and bounds correctly

Working with one-dimensional arrays → An array idea, a Python implementation · Working with one-dimensional arrays → Load and traverse · Working with one-dimensional arrays → Check edge cases

Textbook visit: Read the array idea and traversal sections; use a scalar/string list rather than nested coordinate lists.

Local application: Represent a route as one-dimensional command tokens or scalar distances. State separately how an adapter interprets each item.

Learning check and expected reasoning

For ['A','B','C'], give the first/last valid index and what happens at index 3.

Expected: 0 and 2; index 3 is outside the list. A list of coordinate lists would introduce nested data, not simply a 1D route.

Unit 1 · W4 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Traverse and update a list without confusing value and location

Working with one-dimensional arrays → Load and traverse · Working with one-dimensional arrays → Remember the location of the best value · Working with one-dimensional arrays → Translate the standard algorithms

Textbook visit: Trace a traversal and retained index; distinguish existing array algorithms from extra list-method/API practice.

Local application: Use supplied command-token lists to practise insertion/removal on paper and in Python; linear matching is a local extension, not a new Year 11 assessment requirement by assumption.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Find the first 'B' in ['A','B','B']; give a documented result when no match exists.

Expected: First index 1; choose a consistent not-found sentinel. Explain which index changes during traversal and preserve duplicates.

Unit 1 · W4 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Apply an ordered route list and verify bounds

Working with one-dimensional arrays → Load and traverse · Working with one-dimensional arrays → Check edge cases · Designing and testing solutions → Test: choose evidence that can expose mistakes

Textbook visit: Return to traversal and expected/actual testing; predict which token is read at each index.

Local application: Apply the one-dimensional route to the approved drone/simulator adapter and retain the command/result record; equipment-specific procedures are in the companion pack.

Learning check and expected reasoning

An index equals len(route). May route[index] be accessed? State a preventive condition.

Expected: No; valid indices stop at len(route)-1. Test index < len(route), with a defined policy for an empty route.

Unit 1 · W4 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Explain repeated values, empty input and an index fault

Working with one-dimensional arrays → Remember the location of the best value · Working with one-dimensional arrays → Check edge cases · Working with one-dimensional arrays → Practice and explain · Working with one-dimensional arrays → Practice and explain

Textbook visit: Attempt the existing first-maximum and negative-values questions before revealing answers.

Local application: Dry-run route traversal and a deliberately invalid index; keep algorithm faults separate from hardware response failures.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Why does a maximum initialised to zero fail for [-8,-3], and what should initialise it?

Expected: Zero is not in the data and is larger than both. Use an actual first element after checking non-empty input.

Unit 1 · W5 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Decompose responsibilities into functions with explicit interfaces

Functions and scope → One task, one function · Functions and scope → Return a result · Designing and testing solutions → Use a structure chart and replace a stub

Textbook visit: Read one-task/one-function and the general structure-chart/stub example; do not adopt the chapter's Pygame assessment contract.

Local application: Draw load_route, validate_route and execute_route responsibilities around the local engine; specify inputs/results and retained teacher infrastructure.

Learning check and expected reasoning

What does a stub let you test, and what does it not prove?

Expected: It supplies a predictable interface result so callers can be developed; it does not prove the real input/hardware implementation works.

Unit 1 · W5 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Distinguish parameters, arguments and return values

Functions and scope → Return a result · Functions and scope → Test the part before the whole · Functions and scope → Practice and explain · Functions and scope → Practice and explain

Textbook visit: Answer the existing area/return questions and inspect a pure calculation before using a hardware-facing caller.

Local application: Write a distance/time calculation and a supplied navigation-wrapper call. Define whether it returns a result or changes state.

Learning check and expected reasoning

For def area(width,height) and area(5,2), identify parameters/arguments and the returned product.

Expected: width/height are parameter names; 5/2 are supplied arguments; return value 10 can be used by a caller rather than only printed.

Unit 1 · W5 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Separate local names from shared mutable state

Functions and scope → Names belong to scopes · Functions and scope → Scope faults: trace the name before changing the code · Functions and scope → Trace local and global names · Functions and scope → Practice and explain

Textbook visit: Read scope examples; compare rebinding a local name with changing a passed mutable object.

Local application: Refactor a navigation helper without hidden globals. Predict caller-visible effects before running a small list-mutation example.

Learning check and expected reasoning

If a function assigns local x=9 while global x=2, what remains global? Does that settle how passed lists behave?

Expected: Global x remains 2 without global declaration. Mutable-object changes require separate reasoning; Python is not blanket 'pass by value'.

Unit 1 · W5 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Trace function calls and test a reusable calculation at its boundary

Functions and scope → Test the part before the whole · Functions and scope → Check your reasoning, test the claim and retain the evidence · Functions and scope → Your practical task

Textbook visit: Attempt delivery_charge with the book's stated threshold, then explain a changed boundary independently.

Local application: Use the same contract-testing method on a local engine helper; do not substitute flight success for a function-level expected result.

Learning check and expected reasoning

For order totals 49.99,50,50.01, state the book task's returned charge.

Expected: 5,0,0; correct inclusion at 50. Inputs/outputs stay separate from user prompting so the calculation can be tested.

Unit 1 · W6 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Distinguish persistent files and opening modes

Text files and reliable input → A file outlives the program · Text files and reliable input → Choose the mode deliberately · Text files and reliable input → Read, write and append: three different contracts · Text files and reliable input → Practice and explain

Textbook visit: Read r/w/a contracts and predict a second run's effect before touching practice files.

Local application: Design a telemetry record with named fields and a timestamp convention; use synthetic values for initial practice.

Learning check and expected reasoning

A file contains '7'. What differs when the next run writes '8' using w versus a?

Expected: w replaces existing contents; a preserves existing contents and appends, with delimiters/newlines handled deliberately.

Unit 1 · W6 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Read and validate sequential records

Text files and reliable input → Accept only usable input · Text files and reliable input → Read records in order · Text files and reliable input → Your practical task

Textbook visit: Complete the book's 2,0,5 file-total task, including an empty file, before a multi-field telemetry record.

Local application: Parse a supplied small CSV-style dataset; distinguish the controlled split exercise from a general CSV parser and handle malformed records under an explicit policy.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Predict total for 2,0,5 and an empty file; name a useful conversion-failure test.

Expected: 7 and 0; e.g. 'three' cannot convert to int. A numeric but out-of-range value is a separate validation test.

Unit 1 · W6 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Log observations without inventing missing data

Text files and reliable input → Choose the mode deliberately · Text files and reliable input → Read records in order · Designing and testing solutions → Test: choose evidence that can expose mistakes

Textbook visit: Return to append and record-validation explanations; predict the record count and expected fields.

Local application: Add telemetry logging to the staged engine or simulator; label synthetic versus observed records and keep the raw log unchanged.

Learning check and expected reasoning

A reading is missing. Should the logger replace it with zero and call it observed? Explain.

Expected: No. Use a stated missing-value/error policy; zero may be a genuine measurement and inventing it changes meaning.

Unit 1 · W6 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Handle a file failure and compare error categories

Text files and reliable input → Accept only usable input · Designing and testing solutions → Classify, isolate, repair and retest Python errors · Designing and testing solutions → Compare a paper trace, debugger steps and output probes

Textbook visit: Read targeted error isolation and the debugger/output-probe clinic; record actual observations separately from a paper prediction.

Local application: Test missing file, malformed line and a deliberately wrong accumulator; retain failure, repair and retest evidence.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Distinguish FileNotFoundError, ValueError converting 'three', and a wrong final sum that runs without exception.

Expected: Missing resource, unsuitable conversion, and logic error respectively; use targeted handling/trace evidence rather than a bare catch-all.

Unit 1 · W7 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Evaluate the applied engine against requirements and introduce the event loop

Designing and testing solutions → Test: choose evidence that can expose mistakes · Designing and testing solutions → Evaluate: judge the result against the brief · Repeating work with loops → Repeat while a condition remains true

Textbook visit: Use the general testing/evaluation sections, then the condition-controlled-loop explanation; ignore unrelated game FR IDs.

Local application: Collect individual drone-engine evidence and remaining limitations. Introduce input→update→draw as a different repeated-processing context.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Does a successful run once prove every requirement? Give one boundary/failure case to add.

Expected: No; test stated requirements with normal/boundary/invalid cases and actual evidence. Distinguish a demonstration from complete validation.

Unit 1 · W7 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Run a Pygame window and separate events from held input

Repeating work with loops → Repeat while a condition remains true · Functions and scope → One task, one function · Practice resource

Textbook visit: Use the Pygame preparation lesson's worked stage1_loop with the general loop explanation; it is ungraded teaching material.

Local application: Run the approved practice display; predict motion before changing it; demonstrate Escape and window close without copying assessed game code.

Learning check and expected reasoning

At 160 pixels/s for 250 ms, predict displacement; why is frame count not elapsed seconds?

Expected: 40 pixels; 250 ms is 0.25 seconds and frames may take different times. Process events every frame.

Unit 1 · W7 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Apply selection and bounds to interactive movement

Making decisions with selection → Combine conditions and choices · Working with one-dimensional arrays → Check edge cases · Practice resource

Textbook visit: Revisit conditions and boundary tests; use the supplied state infrastructure without requiring Year 11 authored classes/dictionaries.

Local application: Adapt keyboard movement and a documented screen-bound rule in an unrelated mini-game, then test the edge and just-inside values.

Learning check and expected reasoning

A player is at its maximum allowed x. What should an outward versus inward move do?

Expected: Outward move must remain legal under the stated rule; inward move may change x. Expected positions precede observation.

Unit 1 · W7 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Explain timing/debugging evidence and submit the first component

Designing and testing solutions → Debug: isolate the first incorrect state · Designing and testing solutions → Evaluate: judge the result against the brief · Text files and reliable input → Read records in order

Textbook visit: Use debugging and evaluation vocabulary to review the engine evidence; consult timing references before/after any controlled component only as allowed.

Local application: Submit the local drone-engine component and telemetry explanation; compare active gameplay time with wall-clock pause in a separate practice trace.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Can a high FPS value alone prove that keyboard response met a stated time limit?

Expected: No; measure actual response on the named setup and explain the observation method; state unresolved timing issues honestly.

Unit 1 · W8 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Choose test cases and classify faults before a sprint

Designing and testing solutions → Test: choose evidence that can expose mistakes · Designing and testing solutions → Classify, isolate, repair and retest Python errors · Designing and testing solutions → Compare a paper trace, debugger steps and output probes

Textbook visit: Read the general test/error examples and predict a trace without a key.

Local application: Prepare normal/boundary/invalid tests for an unrelated game mechanic, then perform one debugger observation and retain evidence.

Learning check and expected reasoning

A counter resets inside a loop. Which observation first exposes the error and what regression cases follow?

Expected: The second pass loses earlier state; move initialisation before the loop and retest normal, empty and negative-data cases as applicable.

Unit 1 · W8 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Use collisions, lists and score updates in a small worked game

Working with one-dimensional arrays → Load and traverse · Making decisions with selection → 4. Trace it yourself · Practice resource

Textbook visit: Work through the supplied station collection lab; predict repeat contact and edge-touch behaviour.

Local application: Complete a faded rule in the unrelated practice game; separate drawing from scoring and keep fixtures independent of the hackathon brief.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Under the supplied overlap rule, should touching edges score? Should repeated contact score twice?

Expected: No edge-only collision; an already-collected station adds no second score. State the rule and show normal/boundary tests.

Unit 1 · W8 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Complete a bounded independent prototype and file task

Text files and reliable input → Choose the mode deliberately · Designing and testing solutions → Design: divide the solution into modules · Practice resource

Textbook visit: Consult file-mode/design references before the timed practice; retain an independent attempt before viewing worked solutions.

Local application: Run the 50-minute micro-game sprint with only taught mechanics and provided infrastructure; test append-once results and missing history.

Learning check and expected reasoning

What should happen to history when the result screen is drawn twice for one completed game?

Expected: One final result appended, not one per draw; missing/malformed history follows its documented policy. Explain the state transition that owns saving.

Unit 1 · W8 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Review sources, responsibilities and readiness before the event

Software, ownership and licensing → Read the licence before reuse · Software, ownership and licensing → Keep a source record · Designing and testing solutions → Evaluate: judge the result against the brief

Textbook visit: Inspect licence/source-record guidance and use the evaluation section to identify supported versus independent work.

Local application: Moderate practice evidence, agree team roles and run an individual changed-rule check; finalise the event plan and permitted support.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Does crediting a source automatically give permission to copy it, or prove you authored its logic?

Expected: No; licence permission and acknowledgement are distinct, and independent understanding needs its own evidence.

Unit 1 · W9 L1 · event checkpoint

Learning intention: Interpret the revealed brief and define a tested scope

Designing and testing solutions → Investigate: understand the problem · Designing and testing solutions → Build and revise a Gantt schedule · Designing and testing solutions → Use a structure chart and replace a stub

Textbook visit: At the event's requirements/design checkpoint, consult the general problem definition, Gantt and module-design sections as the event rules permit.

Local application: Day 1 brief reveal: record shared requirements, data design, responsibilities and expected tests for the local hackathon. This row is a checkpoint, not an extra 55-minute period.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Name one required behaviour, one excluded extra and one test that would distinguish a failure.

Expected: Answers refer to the actual issued brief and an observable result; do not import the book's unrelated default game rules.

Unit 1 · W9 L2 · event checkpoint

Learning intention: Implement a small working slice and retain individual evidence

Functions and scope → One task, one function · Working with one-dimensional arrays → Load and traverse · Designing and testing solutions → Develop: build a small working part

Textbook visit: Use targeted function/traversal/development references during the permitted build checkpoint.

Local application: Day 1 build: integrate a small playable slice and retain individual contributions, versions, issues and assistance received.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Can each team member explain one changed function and predict a new input's result independently?

Expected: Evidence names the actual contribution, contract and changed-case prediction; team membership alone does not establish mastery.

Unit 1 · W9 L3 · event checkpoint

Learning intention: Integrate mechanics and run meaningful tests

Designing and testing solutions → Test: choose evidence that can expose mistakes · Designing and testing solutions → Debug: isolate the first incorrect state · Text files and reliable input → Choose the mode deliberately

Textbook visit: Return to general testing/debugging/file guidance during the event's integration/QA checkpoint.

Local application: Day 2 integration: run planned tests, isolate one real failure and retest earlier behaviour; retain actual results and unfinished work.

Learning check and expected reasoning

What must a useful failed-test record contain beyond 'did not work'?

Expected: Initial state/input, independent expected result, actual result, build/version, cause/repair and retest/regression outcome.

Unit 1 · W9 L4 · event checkpoint

Learning intention: Defend and evaluate the solution using evidence

Designing and testing solutions → Evaluate: judge the result against the brief · Software, ownership and licensing → Keep a source record

Textbook visit: Before the pitch and after code lock as permitted, use evaluation/source-record criteria; do not edit locked work.

Local application: Day 2 pitch/demo/code defence: link decisions to requirements, identify individual work and limitations. Event hours are recorded separately from the four checkpoints.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Does a five-minute team pitch prove 100% individual mastery? What extra evidence is needed?

Expected: No; individual explanation/change task, contribution/version records and appropriate teacher authentication complement the team product.

Unit 1 · W10 L1 · controlled practical

Learning intention: Demonstrate individual programming skills under controlled conditions

Unit 1 consolidation → Station B: algorithms in two representations · Unit 1 consolidation → Station C: debug and prove the correction · Text files and reliable input → Read records in order

Textbook visit: Preparation links only: use before the test; revisit after collection, not during closed-book conditions unless expressly allowed.

Local application: Task 2: 50-minute programming practical plus five minutes setup/collection; assess only taught and independently practised operations.

Learning check and expected reasoning

After collection, identify one submitted trace/test decision and an assumption that affected it.

Expected: Explanation matches the submitted version; original work stays distinct from later correction. No textbook access is assumed during the test.

Unit 1 · W10 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Explain network resources and choose transmission media

Network foundations → A shared set of rules · Addresses, devices and media → Choose a medium for the setting

Textbook visit: Use the shared-rules introduction and media comparisons during the post-test debrief/new-network lesson.

Local application: Inspect the pod's wired/wireless/fibre paths and relate each to distance/capacity/interference needs, rather than product names.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Give one reason to choose fibre between buildings and one reason for copper at a desk.

Expected: Justify against actual link requirements; distance, capacity and electrical interference differ by medium and installation.

Unit 1 · W10 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Distinguish nominal capacity, achieved rate and impairments

Addresses, devices and media → Choose a medium for the setting · Designing and protecting a network → Find the bottleneck · Network scenarios and review → Practice and explain

Textbook visit: Read medium/bottleneck reasoning and attempt the existing idealised transfer calculation.

Local application: Compare supplied synthetic throughput results with a named local observation if available; discuss attenuation, EMI and crosstalk through companion evidence.

Learning check and expected reasoning

In an ideal transfer, how long is 80 megabits over 20 megabits/s? Does that guarantee real elapsed time?

Expected: 4 seconds ideally; real throughput/overhead/contention/latency may differ. Use bits and seconds consistently.

Unit 1 · W10 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Interpret a physical-link demonstration without treating it as complete diagnosis

Addresses, devices and media → Choose a medium for the setting · Network scenarios and review → Use a repeatable explanation

Textbook visit: Read medium-selection and repeatable-explanation sections before the approved physical demonstration.

Local application: Observe the teacher-managed fibre demonstration using the companion procedure; distinguish visible continuity evidence from measured performance or a full certification test.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Does a continuity observation prove a link meets all throughput and reliability requirements?

Expected: No; state what was observed and what further measurement/specification is needed. Do not invent test results.

Unit 1 · W11 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Relate cable layout and pair conventions to a declared requirement

Addresses, devices and media → Choose a medium for the setting · Designing and protecting a network → Scale and logical diagrams

Textbook visit: Use general media/logical-versus-physical distinctions; consult the separate labelled pinout reference for hands-on detail.

Local application: Compare supplied T568A/B diagrams and the required straight-through mapping before the cabling lab; equipment details are enrichment, not a hidden textbook prerequisite.

Learning check and expected reasoning

For a straight-through teaching fixture, what is the expected numbered-pin mapping?

Expected: 1→1 through 8→8 under the specified fixture; a correct drawing must label both ends and its chosen convention.

Unit 1 · W11 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Document a physical build and distinguish it from a diagram

Addresses, devices and media → Choose a medium for the setting · Designing and testing solutions → Test: choose evidence that can expose mistakes

Textbook visit: Revisit requirements and expected/actual test planning before constructing a cable.

Local application: Measure/terminate the approved Cat6 practice cable using the companion procedure; record individual work, inspection and subsequent tester result.

Learning check and expected reasoning

What evidence distinguishes 'I planned the cable' from 'I built and tested it'?

Expected: A labelled plan plus actual build identity and observed test result; a simulated result is not evidence of physical termination.

Unit 1 · W11 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Trace connections through patching and switching components

Addresses, devices and media → Choose a device for its function · Designing and protecting a network → Scale and logical diagrams

Textbook visit: Read device roles and logical diagrams; annotate the data path independently of cabinet layout.

Local application: Use the pod patch-panel/punch-down activity as the local application; draw host→panel→switch path and identify connection points using the companion guide.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Expected: No; distinguish passive termination/patching from active forwarding. Trace each link rather than naming the rack as one device.

Unit 1 · W11 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Diagnose evidence from a cable test and plan a retest

Network scenarios and review → Use a repeatable explanation · Designing and testing solutions → Debug: isolate the first incorrect state

Textbook visit: Use the explain/observe/hypothesise/test method; consult the companion tester fixture and actual instrument guide.

Local application: Classify synthetic maps: all pins straight; pin 3 open; pins 1/3 and 2/6 exchanged. Then compare with an observed local test where available.

Learning check and expected reasoning

For a required straight-through cable, classify 3→open and 1→3,2→6,3→1,6→2 mappings.

Expected: Open conductor versus incorrect mapping for the stated requirement; identify affected endpoints and retest after repair. Do not infer every fault from one LED pattern.

Unit 1 · W12 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Explain topology and network-layer responsibilities

Network foundations → Four layers, four responsibilities · Designing and protecting a network → Scale and logical diagrams

Textbook visit: Build the four-layer stack from the general chapter; read the separate seven-layer comparison only as a labelled extension.

Local application: Annotate star/mesh/bus/hybrid diagrams and compare logical versus physical topology; avoid making model names substitute for functions.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Place HTTP, TCP, IP and Ethernet in the four-layer model and explain a responsibility for each.

Expected: Application service, transport delivery, internet routing/addressing and link frame delivery. Relate model labels to functions.

Unit 1 · W12 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Distinguish local link operation from end-to-end service

Textbook visit: Read device and diagnostic explanations before checking links.

Local application: Interconnect approved pod components through copper/fibre adapters; record physical/link observations before testing applications.

Learning check and expected reasoning

A ping succeeds. Does that prove the website works? Give one further relevant check.

Unit 1 · W12 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Use network and host portions rather than address-class guesses

Addresses, devices and media → Addresses and the local network · Numbers and characters in a computer → Place value changes with the base · Numbers and characters in a computer → Hexadecimal is a compact notation · Addresses, devices and media → Practice and explain

Textbook visit: Read local-network comparison and retrieve binary/hex place values; compare addresses using the stated mask.

Local application: Use a small /24 addressing table for the pod; historical class labels are background, not the rule for interpreting an explicit prefix.

Learning check and expected reasoning

Are 192.168.20.10 and 192.168.21.10 local under 255.255.255.0? Why?

Expected: No; their /24 network portions differ. Use the actual mask/prefix, not only the first address octet.

Unit 1 · W12 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Use addressing and diagnostic observations to test a hypothesis

Addresses, devices and media → Addresses and the local network · Addresses, devices and media → Gateways: next-hop routing versus protocol translation · Network foundations → Encapsulation and diagnostic tools

Local application: Configure the isolated practice interfaces under the companion instructions; inspect a supplied ICMP trace and then an authorised local observation.

Learning check and expected reasoning

A host is 192.168.40.12/24 and its gateway is 192.168.41.1. What should be checked first?

Expected: Gateway is outside the host's ordinary local /24; verify intended addressing/interface configuration before inferring an external outage.

Unit 1 · W13 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Choose a device by its network function

Textbook visit: Read NIC/switch/router/AP functions and label a path in the logical diagram.

Local application: Identify components in the pod and map them to host connectivity, LAN forwarding, routing and wireless access.

Expected: AP for wireless LAN access; router/L3 function for network boundaries. Brand names do not establish function.

Unit 1 · W13 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Explain switch forwarding using observed or supplied evidence

Unit 1 · W13 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Explain host configuration, gateway and dynamic address allocation

Addresses, devices and media → Addresses and the local network · Addresses, devices and media → Gateways: next-hop routing versus protocol translation · Designing and protecting a network → Protect against unauthorised access

Textbook visit: Read host/mask/gateway responsibilities; use the companion lease/configuration example for DHCP operations.

Local application: Inspect/configure an approved isolated router address pool and gateway; check reserved/network/broadcast addresses and unique leases.

Unit 1 · W13 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Interpret a lease exchange as evidence, not a memorised label list

Local application: Read a supplied Discover→Offer→Request→Acknowledgement trace, then compare a real permitted capture if available.

Unit 1 · W14 L1 · controlled theory

Learning intention: Demonstrate networking knowledge under controlled conditions

Network scenarios and review → Use a repeatable explanation · Network scenarios and review → Review task: the library upgrade · Unit 1 exam preparation → Use the practice paper

Learning check and expected reasoning

After collection, identify one response that needed a scenario-specific causal explanation rather than a device name.

Expected: Original answer and a missing/present fact-to-reasoning link are identified; later corrections remain separate.

Unit 1 · W14 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Explain wireless performance using requirements and evidence

Addresses, devices and media → Choose a medium for the setting · Designing and protecting a network → Find the bottleneck · Network scenarios and review → Use a repeatable explanation

Local application: Compare supplied channel/interference scenarios and observed results where available; distinguish radio band from an automatic speed guarantee.

Unit 1 · W14 L3 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Map identity, access and wireless controls to a precise configuration

Unit 1 · W14 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Interpret signal measurements without overclaiming their meaning

Unit 1 · W15 L1 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Diagnose programming and networking weaknesses from evidence

Textbook visit: Complete a short selection of the existing diagnostic/stations before reading answers.

Unit 1 · W15 L2 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Translate unfamiliar requirements into an algorithm and explanation

Unit 1 · W15 L3 · ordinary lesson

Unit 1 · W15 L4 · ordinary lesson

Learning intention: Attempt timed mixed practice and explain corrections

Unit 1 · W16 L1 · ordinary lesson

Unit 1 · W16 L3 · exam block

Unit 1 · W16 L4 · exam block

Local application: Final block and collection of the same examination; reserve the administration allowance. If periods are non-contiguous, the school must arrange a suitable continuous session.

Learning check and expected reasoning

In later feedback, choose one changed retry from an actual misconception without rewriting the original as if it were submitted.

Expected: Original examination evidence, correction and later independent retry are distinct; actual exam scheduling/approval remains a school decision.
